newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Solana to take NATO crusade to Central Asia.
newsitem.headline: Solana to take NATO crusade to Central Asia.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, on a diplomatic blitz ahead of NATO's plans to expand into eastern Europe this summer, starts a tour of former Soviet republics in Central Asia on Monday.
His week-long tour of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan will start in the Kazakh capital Almaty after a brief visit to Moscow on Sunday.
"The Secretary-General will arrive on March 10. He will meet (President Nursulatan) Nazarbayev and defence officials," a foreign ministry spokesman said.

Officials said Solana would discuss the involvement of the four republics in NATO's "Partnership for Peace" programme, which plans 10 days of joint peacekeeping exercises in September in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.
Solana's visit comes as Russia and NATO are sparring over the alliance's plans to admit former Communist countries in eastern Europe -- expected to be the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary.
In Moscow, he is scheduled to meet Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, a strong critic of NATO expansion plans, to work on a document regarding Russia's security.
The four Asian states have different attitudes toward the war of words between Moscow and NATO.
Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan say NATO's expansion eastwards must not be hasty and Russia's interests must be taken into account.
"NATO's hasty progress eastwards is not a reasonable policy towards Russia," Kazakhstan's Nazarbayev said last week.

"I think...such a hurry of the West does not favour (Russia's) democratic forces," the Kazakh leader said in a clear reference Russia's ultra-nationalists and communists whipping up passions over NATO's expansion plans.
Kyrgyz President Askar Akayev said that as his country considers Russia its main strategic partner, it shares Moscow's concerns.

"This is why we think that Russia's interests, which are directly in Europe, must be taken into account in all NATO's geopolitical actions and plans," Akayev told Russia's Interfax news agency earlier this week.
Uzbekistan, whose strongman President Islam Karimov has been trying to pursue an independent policy since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, was far less concerned about NATO plans.
Karimov, who rarely grants interviews at home, said during an official visit to the Czech Republic in January that his country objected to Moscow's attempts to block the expansion.
"We do not see that NATO should be a threat for the post-Soviet region," he said.
The position of secretive Turkmenistan remains unclear. The country's President Saparmurat Niyazov, who enjoys a Soviet- style personality cult, likes to boast of Turkmenistan's official neutrality.
But Russian officers serve in Turkmenistan to help guard the country's border with Iran and Afghanistan, and Niyazov calls Russia "a strategic partner".

Russia also keeps a contingent of around 20,000 peacekeepers and border guards in Tajikistan and views its troops in the region as a bulwark against the advent of militant Islam from nearby Afghanistan.
On Saturday, Russian border forces in Tajikistan killed six people trying to cross the border and a Russian base in the capital Dushanbe came under fire although no one was hurt, officials said.
